anchor: Ada's spine as it stands (commons/maps/curriculum_spine.json v1.5: 25 sequences, 204 working-tree halls), which follows introductory Processing (spine 1-5) and The Nature of Code (spine 6-21) with Ada-only blocks (formfinding, shaders, isosurfaces, boolean, graphs) and the crisis arc (23-25). The braid is applied chapter by chapter; no chapter is moved out of spine order.
title: The Spine as It Stands: a braided course in the museum's order (control)
thesis: You will learn to program by walking Ada's museum in the order it is built. It opens as Paul Klee's point going for a walk and as the first semester every creative-coding course teaches: one body, a variable, a boundary, a frame, a measured relation, a recorded walk, a loop, a surface, a class, a pattern. Each idea makes a body you can stand on, walk through, carry or become. It continues as The Nature of Code: bodies that change, are thrown, balance, swing, happen by chance, fill space as noise, grow by rules, go soft, blur into fields, flock and learn. It ends where no coding course goes: graphs, the foundations crisis, the QFEP laboratory and the world outside the lab. Every chapter asks the same things. Build a body in code. Turn it into a family with one axis. Write down which two members will look most alike before you render them, then make the comparison image and one sentence it supports. Put the body where a body meets it. Then say what the approximation owes. This order is one choice among several: chance, noise and sound arrive late here, where The Nature of Code and Aesthetic Programming put chance early. The course keeps the museum's order so every hall you visit is the one you are learning in, and so you can see what the other orders would change.

parts.title: I. The point goes for a walk (spine 1: primitives)
parts.promise: You make one body from code, give it a boundary, place it in a frame, measure it against another, record its walk, repeat it on a grid, build a surface from vertices and pay for smoothness, and ship a first build.

parts.title: II. Frame, many, colour, pattern (spine 2-5)
parts.promise: You pose bodies in time, walk in a body of your own (scanned or built), make many from one scene, colour them by a rule written in a class, and read one pattern source under several laws, saved to disk.

parts.title: III. Change, force, balance, wave (spine 6-9)
parts.promise: You let bodies change: a curve becomes steps, forces throw and hold bodies, stacks stand or fall, a pendulum becomes a circle, a spiral stair and a sound.

parts.title: IV. Chance, field, pixel (spine 10-12)
parts.promise: You make chance repeatable, give it a distribution and a round of play, turn it into a walkable field, and move a rule into the GPU, saying each time what the approximation owes.

parts.title: V. Rules that grow, bodies without edges (spine 13-19)
parts.promise: You write rules that grow bodies (neighbour rules, recursion, grammars, generators) and bodies without fixed edges (soft, implicit, carved), and keep each one stopped, budgeted and walkable.

parts.title: VI. Bodies that choose, and the crisis (spine 20-25)
parts.promise: You build bodies that choose (flocks, learners, routes), stage what mathematics cannot close, measure your own predictions, and leave the lab with a finished hall.

tracks.title: Three weeks: a body family in your own hall
tracks.length: 3 weeks full time (15 days). Week 1: chapters 1+2 (day 1), 3, 4, 5+6, 7. Week 2: chapters 10, 12, 15, 23, 25. Week 3: mini project from day 11, with guest and critique sessions (Code Societies' rhythm) and the showing on day 15. SUPPLIED AND NAMED, because the track skips the chapter that teaches them: defining functions (ch. 8) - met first by reading the AI-written check_magic() in ch. 10; delta (ch. 11) - read inside the supplied walker in ch. 12; MultiMesh (ch. 14) - the 10 PRINT walls in ch. 23 come from a supplied wall-emitter helper; PackedVector3Array and SurfaceTool (ch. 8, 14) - the terrain in ch. 25 is emitted by a supplied terrain_mesh(points) helper whose inputs and output are stated; surfaces from vertices and smooth normals (ch. 8-9) - bodies are built from primitive meshes and SphereMesh resolution instead; rotation order (ch. 11) - Inspector rotation only; scene instancing (ch. 13) - duplicated nodes; the RigidBody drop in ch. 3 and the XR staging scene - supplied throughout.
tracks.mini_project: Extrapolated body (after Code as Creative Medium): one body built in code (primitives in loops, a noise field, or around your imported scan), exposed as a family with one @export axis of 3-5 values; the closest pair predicted in writing before rendering; one comparison image and a one-sentence claim; one debt comment in the code saying what the approximation owes; placed in your hall where a visitor stands on, walks through, carries or becomes it; shown on desktop, and on the headset if the route works. Optional variant after Blas' Facial Weaponization Suite: aggregate the class's scans into one collective body, axis = number of scans (consent first; matched topology is needed).

tracks.title: One year: the museum in order, and a hall of your own
tracks.length: About a year: two semesters, 39 chapters at roughly one a week, with checkpoints CP1 (ch. 10), CP2 (ch. 16), a midterm simulation project (ch. 22), CP4 (ch. 26), a pause week (ch. 33), the final project planned at ch. 36 and shown at ch. 39.
tracks.mini_project: Final project: a finished hall in the endless museum with at least three body families, each with prediction, comparison image, claim and a debt comment in the code; walked by classmates on desktop and headset; exported.

chapters.title: Day Zero: a world that runs, and breaks
chapters.body: The supplied base scene (floor, sun, camera, WorldEnvironment, a Label3D) opened, run and stopped. The student's first body is the greeting that stands in the room: its text set by one statement, printed to Output. Then one planted typo, and Godot's exact message read aloud. Supplied: base.tscn and the XR staging scene (named, opened later).

argument.axis: camera standpoint on the same scene (Inspector values only)
argument.predict: Front and floor level look most alike: both see the label's face over the floor. From above the label is a thin sliver; from behind the text reads mirrored (Label3D is double-sided by default [mem]). [P]
argument.claim: A scene is not a picture: the same bodies give different stills, and one standpoint can nearly hide a body.

chapters.debt: The default scene is a set of decisions nobody in the room made: a sun, a floor at y = 0, a camera at standing eye height, English keywords (FLOW-MATIC's default, Marino ch. 5). Montfort's 'Critique My Starter Programs' turned on the starter scene: which body does it assume? Errors are help: 'valid and intentional are different' (Montfort ch. 4).
chapters.place: Run it on the desktop; then follow the written headset route with the supplied XR staging scene and stand in the room you just changed.

chapters.body: A column that grows: a box in the scene whose height is a variable, set once in _ready() and changed in _process(); a Label3D prints the count beside the supplied frame_counter_display.

argument.axis: where and how the height is written
argument.predict: The first two are identical in every still, although one runs once and the other 60-90 times a second; the two accumulating columns differ tenfold after the same time. [P]
argument.claim: A picture cannot show code that runs without changing anything; only accumulation makes time visible.

chapters.debt: Growth counted in frames belongs to the machine: at 90 Hz in the headset the += column grows 1.5 times faster than at 60 Hz on a laptop. The repair (delta) is held back to chapter 11, and the log should say so. Frames and seconds diverge on frame_counter_display.

chapters.title: Point One: one body from code, and its boundary
chapters.body: A point built entirely in code: MeshInstance3D.new(), SphereMesh.new() (a resource, not a node), add_child(); a StaticBody3D with a CollisionShape3D whose radius is set apart from the visible radius. Supplied: a ball that drops (opened in chapter 18).

argument.axis: collider radius relative to the visible radius
argument.predict: Without the dropped ball all four look identical. With it, 0.5x and 'no collider' look most alike: in both the ball sinks into the visible body; only 1x shows touching, and 2x makes the ball float. [P]
argument.claim: What a body is to others (its collider) is set apart from what it looks like; touch is a third thing, made only where the two agree.

chapters.debt: Colliders are approximations chosen for speed: sphere, box, convex hull, trimesh; the walker itself is a capsule. Where look and boundary disagree, bodies pass into each other (in this project the walk map cannot see CSG collision [mem project note]). Gaboury's Utah teapot: which primitives are the default bodies, and who standardised them.
chapters.place: Walk into it with the supplied desktop walker: you stop at the collider, not at the surface you see. In the headset, put your hand into the 'no collider' point.

chapters.title: Point Coordinates: position and frame
chapters.body: A point with a parent: its Vector3 position set in code, the parent moved, turned and scaled; position and global_position shown on a label. On the XR route the student makes their own point holdable (no single grab() call, per the ruling).

argument.axis: the parent's transform, child position fixed at (0.5, 0, 0)
argument.predict: Identity and moved look most alike in a still framed on the pair (same shape, same child-parent distance); turned and scaled put the same three numbers somewhere else. [P]
argument.claim: Position is always relative: the same three numbers make a different place under a different parent.

chapters.debt: The origin and the axes are decisions (y up, metres, a world 0,0,0). Far from the origin floats jitter. global_position is a calculation that looks like a fact. Pickup belongs here (ruling), so 'carrying' starts as a change of parent.

chapters.title: Point Lines: distance belongs to the line
chapters.body: A segment between two carried points: d = b - a, d.length(), a label with the number; the connector placed by the supplied show_between() in segment.gd (named, opened in chapter 8).

argument.axis: the measure the connector follows
argument.predict: Euclidean and horizontal look most alike while both points share a height; lift one end and they part. [P]
argument.claim: Distance is a chosen measure, and the measure draws a different connector between the same two points.

chapters.debt: length() hides a geometry: Euclid by default. b - a is a Vector3 (a direction with a size); length() returns a float that forgets the direction (types). The norm returns in NonEuclidean_Spaces (chapter 37).
chapters.place: Two people each hold one end in the headset (or two keys on desktop): the number is a relation between two bodies.

chapters.title: Point Trace: a point goes for a walk
chapters.body: A recorder: a typed Array[Vector3] of kept positions (the list before append), a condition that keeps a position only past a gate distance (the condition before the threshold), a cap, named input actions for pause and clear; the kept positions drawn as dots.

argument.axis: gate distance
argument.predict: 0 and 0.02 m look most alike (a dense line either way; the count differs, the picture barely); 0.5 m reads as a dotted polygon. [P]
argument.claim: A record is a body shaped by what it refuses to keep.

chapters.debt: Every record forgets: the gate and the cap decide which walks survive, and rounding tidies a trembling hand into a line (draw_dot's retention family: none, trace, lattice, archive, wax [V ada.json]).

chapters.title: Many bodies: loops, and a first family
chapters.body: A 5 x 5 lattice of cubes from two nested for-loops; spacing and cube size exposed with @export, so the Inspector turns one grid into a family.

argument.axis: spacing relative to cube size
argument.predict: Overlap and touching look most alike: both read as one slab, and only gaps make the count visible. [P]
argument.claim: At or below touching, many bodies read as one: a grid's number is only visible through its gaps.

chapters.debt: The Cartesian lattice is the default order of 3D space ('purely repetitive and therefore structural', Klee I.6). Twenty-five colliders cost more than one. The grid is not a prerequisite for the first line (ruling), yet it becomes everyone's floor.
chapters.place: Stand on it: overlap and touching carry the walker, gaps drop it between cubes, scatter is a field of stepping stones.
godot: for i in range(n); nested loops
the Inspector as the family's control panel

chapters.title: Surfaces from vertices: the triangle
chapters.body: make_face(a, b, c): three Vector3s submitted to an ImmediateMesh, then to SurfaceTool; a fan loop makes a polygon; Polythedra's open trihedron closed by a convex hull from the same points. The supplied show_between() from chapter 5 is opened and rewritten as the student's own function.

argument.axis: one corner walked toward collinearity
argument.predict: Needle and collinear look most alike from the front: both read as a line, although one still has area. [P]
argument.claim: A surface is three points that disagree; when they agree, the face vanishes.

chapters.debt: A face has one side: Godot winds front faces clockwise and culls the back (Gaboury, 'Culling Vision' [V research_engine]). The triangle is the only polygon the GPU believes; every curved body is owed to it.
chapters.place: Walk behind the triangle and it disappears; give the polyhedron a ConvexPolygonShape3D and stand on it.

chapters.title: Budget of smoothness: from pyramid to sphere
chapters.body: build_ring(n) returns n points on a circle from sin and cos; a pyramid on that ring with @export base_sides; the same builder stacked into a sphere of rings and segments; flat against smooth normals with SurfaceTool.generate_normals().

argument.axis: sphere tessellation (declared on sphere_high: coarse, low, high, ultra) [V ada.json]
argument.predict: High and ultra look most alike at arm's length: past a few hundred triangles the eye stops counting while the count keeps multiplying. [P]
argument.claim: Smoothness is bought with triangles, and past a point the price keeps rising while the picture stops changing.

chapters.debt: Polycount against smooth deformation, the 2023 application's own question (l. 89). A smooth-looking sphere is a polyhedron whose normals lie about its facets. Counting triangles is not measuring frame time (measured in chapter 25). Primitives_Portals: the gap to the true circle never reaches zero.
chapters.place: In the headset, stand in a ring of spheres: too many 'ultra' bodies make the room stutter at 72-90 Hz, and comfort is part of the budget.

chapters.title: Melencolia: primitives synthesis and a first build
chapters.body: Duerer's truncated pyramid assembled from snap_pyramid_puzzle's parts; check_magic(NUMBERS) over rows, columns and diagonals; a custom signal emitted when an arrangement completes and heard by the room. check_magic() is first written with an AI assistant under stated constraints, then checked.

argument.axis: pyramid apex (declared on snap_pyramid_puzzle: tall, regular, flat, spire, inverted) [V ada.json]
argument.predict: Tall and spire look most alike (both read as needles); inverted is the outlier because its silhouette and shadow flip. [P]
argument.claim: One base and one apex make a family whose members read as different kinds of object: roof, tent, spire, funnel.

chapters.debt: ai_assist as debt: before accepting the generated code, write what should change, what must not, and what observation would show it is wrong; code you did not write is a black box you now own. Melencolia's solid has been argued over for 500 years: a body can be exact and still undecided.

chapters.title: Pose in time: move, turn, scale
chapters.body: A jointed body of pivots: each plank a child Node3D turned by a Basis about its own pivot, moved by lerp on a delta-accumulated clock (the Trans_Pre pickup's bob and spin). Chapter 2's column is repaired with += rate * delta.

argument.axis: order of two 90-degree turns applied to one plank lying along x (global axes)
argument.predict: 'x then y' and 'y only' look most alike: the x turn spins the plank about its own length, so both end up along z (one on edge, one flat); 'y then x' stands the plank upright. [P]
argument.claim: Rotation does not commute: the same two turns in another order make another pose.

chapters.debt: One turn, three encodings (Euler angles, Basis, quaternion) and gimbal lock; a pose is nine numbers that mean nothing alone. delta repairs frame dependence, but the physics tick still quantises time.
chapters.place: Ride it: an AnimatableBody3D plank turns about a pivot you choose while the walker stands on it.

chapters.title: The body you walk in
chapters.body: The supplied walker opened: a CharacterBody3D with move_and_slide() and a Camera3D at its eye. Its skin is replaced by the student's own imported body (a phone 3D scan, a Tilt Brush sculpture or a Blender model as glTF), with the capsule collider kept.

argument.axis: what is scaled, seen from the walker's camera
argument.predict: Room x4 and body x0.25 give nearly identical stills from the walker's eye; only the doorways the small body now fits through tell them apart. 'Both x4' looks like 'nothing'. [P]
argument.claim: Scale is relative: from inside, a bigger room and a smaller you make the same picture, and only collision tells them apart.

chapters.debt: The capsule is the engine's default body (about 1.8 m, upright; in VR two hands); the scan is heavy (often 100k+ triangles) and its skin does not collide; the camera height encodes a body. 'Critique My Starter Programs' again: which body does the starter assume?
chapters.place: Become it: walk as your scanned body. In the headset the desktop walker is swapped for the XR body; the skin stays a child of the controller (skin vs controller, GDQuest 3D module 7 [V research_engine]).

chapters.title: Many bodies with addresses
chapters.body: The Trans_Pre pickup saved as a scene and instanced from a 2D array by nested loops; each pickup an Area3D; collecting writes 0 into its slot. molnar_cube_study is visited with its disorder supplied (random is met in chapter 23).

argument.axis: what collecting does to the address
argument.predict: Keep, hide and queue_free are indistinguishable in a still (gaps where collected); erase-and-shift rebuilds the row with the gaps closed. [P]
argument.claim: A picture cannot tell an empty address from a hidden body; only the data, and what a body can still touch, can.

chapters.debt: Hiding is not deleting: a hidden Area3D still reports and still costs. The address outlives the occupant (the sequence's own question: does removing an occupant erase its address or change what a body can stand on? [V ada.json]). chapters.title: A floor that keeps time: MultiMesh and sound
chapters.body: A 16 x 16 MultiMesh floor, monochrome (coloured Disco returns after Color, per the array_tutorial ruling), stepped by a delta clock; each step plays a tone generated into an AudioStreamWAV from a PackedByteArray.

argument.axis: step rule over (x, z, phase)
argument.predict: Checker and stripes look most alike in any one still (half the cells lit, regular); 'every cell' is the outlier, all or nothing. [P]
argument.claim: One clock and four index rules: the floor's pattern is arithmetic on an address, and time only shifts it.

chapters.debt: A MultiMesh draws 256 instances in one call, but they are not nodes: no collider, no signal each (a crowd without individuals). A generated tone is a list of numbers the speaker must trust.
chapters.place: Dance on it: an Area3D under the walker shifts the phase when you step.

chapters.title: Colour by a rule: describe a body in a single class
chapters.body: chroma_stack rebuilt as the student's own class_name: a const Dictionary of stacks, an @export_enum rule, a loop that turns the recipe into PrimitiveMesh parts, each given a StandardMaterial3D coloured by the rule. The prompt is CCSWG's 'describe a body in a single class'.

argument.axis: colour rule (declared on chroma_stack: one, by_shape, by_height, by_neighbour, composed) [V ada.json]
argument.predict: by_shape and by_height look most alike on the bauhaus stack, because its shapes are stacked in height order and both rules paint the same parts; 'one' is the outlier. [P]
argument.claim: A colour rule reads a body's structure back to you, or hides it when two structures coincide.

chapters.debt: Colour is relative (Albers): one material reads differently under coloured light (Color_Flashlight). StandardMaterial3D's default albedo is the default body of surfaces; sRGB against linear and the headset's display shift colour without an error. Which properties get a place in the class is the modelling choice, and the critique.
chapters.place: Walk round the stack with a coloured flashlight: colour belongs to the meeting of light, surface and eye.

chapters.title: Pattern: one source, many laws
chapters.body: A 4 x 4 palette-index source read by get_color(x, y) under a wallpaper rule, baked into an Image and ImageTexture and laid on a floor, a wall and a garment mesh by UV; the source saved and restored as versioned JSON in user://. Tutorial_Pattern's shader version is visited as supplied (shaders are met in chapter 26).

argument.axis: wallpaper rule over the same 4 x 4 source
argument.predict: pm and pg look most alike (both mirror; pg only shifts the mirrored rows by half a block); p1 is the outlier for a motif with a strong direction. [P]
argument.claim: One motif under four laws gives four patterns: the pattern is the rule, not the tile.

chapters.debt: The symmetry census claims completeness (17 groups) where Klee argues for non-symmetrical balance (II.23). A texture is a skin with no thickness and no collision; UV seams show where a curved body was cut to lie flat. The spine keeps regularity here and randomness five sequences later, though 10 PRINT argues you need the grid to see chance.

argument.claim: An impossible body is possible from one standpoint: the camera, not the geometry, closes the loop.

chapters.debt: Goedel and the halting problem: 'not found within budget' is not 'unprovable' (Godel_Incompleteness). A bool is a two-valued decision; a third value is a political choice (non-binary logic in code). Non-Euclidean space in a Euclidean engine is always a trick, a shader warp the collider does not follow (return of chapter 5's norm).

chapters.title: Order toward entropy: the QFEP laboratory
chapters.body: The student's own course log as data: each chapter's predicted closest pair against the measured one, logged into a PackedFloat32Array and drawn as a line chart (F = |prediction - observation|, as QFEP_F_Term does); E as the spread (RMS) of a Brownian population; lambda from the visitor's position along a track driving a MultiMesh field.

argument.axis: lambda, order to entropy (lambda_hall)
argument.predict: 0.7 and 1.0 look most alike: disorder saturates, and past a point more entropy adds no visible difference; 0.35 is where structure and noise are both legible. [P]
argument.claim: Entropy saturates: the step from order to some disorder is visible, the step from much to more is not.

chapters.debt: A metric is a body too: F measures my prediction error, not the world. QFEP is a framework, not a law (the Sieve's third question: what lives in the dark spot?). Entropy as resistance (Haraway and Ahmed via Queer 3D).

chapters.title: Leaving the lab: situated computation and your hall
chapters.body: room_shape_demonstrator: seating generated by loops under a plan, checked by a raycast sightline from every seat to one point; the final hall reads back a record another hall wrote (a user:// file, written atomically), so state survives scenes and restarts.

argument.axis: seating plan (declared on room_shape_demonstrator: pair, head, circle, panopticon, vacant) [V ada.json]
argument.predict: Head and panopticon look most alike from above (every chair faces one point); circle is the plan where the sightline check passes for every seat. [P]
argument.claim: Equal spacing is not equal standing: a plan decides who sees whom.

chapters.debt: Algorithmic bias (Buolamwini's Coded Gaze, in the application). Accessibility as a check the code can run but not decide. The course's own dark spot: 'revealing the black box' can hide as much as it shows (Chun's 'sourcery', Programmed Visions ch. 1).

learned_from: Processing Handbook, Learning Processing, NYU ICM [V research_creative]: spine 1-5 already is creative coding's 27-year intro order (draw, variables, conditions, loops, functions, objects, arrays). The control keeps it and borrows ICM's double titles (effect, then idea: 'Many bodies: loops, and a first family').

The Nature of Code [V research_creative]: spine 6-21 is NoC reordered; the control keeps its inanimate-to-living-to-intelligence drift, its cumulative chapter-end project (the Ecosystem exhibit becomes 'your hall in the endless museum') and the ITP course's midterm simulation project (after chapter 22).

Aesthetic Programming [V research_ccs]: RunMe/ReadMe becomes BODY plus ARGUMENT, with Ada's falsifiable prediction replacing the open ReadMe questions; the ReadMe lives beside the code in Git; peer feedback on each chapter; a pause week with no new syntax (chapter 33); the final project planned two units before the end (chapter 36).

Critical Code Studies (Marino) [V research_ccs]: code-critique stations at the DEBT step, on Ada's own approximating code (the RNG in chapter 23, the FastNoiseLite call in 25, the marching-cubes table in 32), after the Kittler raytracer chapter; the Climategate 'confessing comment' becomes a debt comment in the student's own code (detail [mem]).
CCSWG 2024 [V research_ccs]: 'describe a body in a single class' as the classes chapter's prompt (chapter 15); write first, critique second inside every chapter.

Montfort, Exploratory Programming [V research_ccs]: errors in week one as a positive topic ('valid and intentional are different', chapter 1's planted bug); 'Critique My Starter Programs' turned on Godot's default scene (chapter 1) and capsule player (chapter 12).

10 PRINT [V research_ccs]: 'Maze Walker' as the first seeded body (chapter 23); 'Regularity before Randomness' is quoted against the control itself, which keeps the grid (5) and chance (10) five sequences apart and says so.

Fuller's Software Studies: A Lexicon [V research_ccs]: one reading per code idea, pulled in by the code rather than pushed by a theory sequence (Variable ch. 2, Lists ch. 6, Loop ch. 7, Function ch. 8, Import/Export ch. 12, Object Orientation ch. 15, Glitch ch. 25, Pixel ch. 26, Elegance ch. 28).

Albers, Interaction of Color [V research_bauhaus]: the argument strand's ancestor ('make two colours look alike' becomes 'predict which two bodies look alike'); a constrained material (one body with one or two exposed axes) keeps comparisons honest.

Klee, Pedagogical Sketchbook, corrected order [V research_bauhaus, lineage.json]: Part I (line, structure, body) is spine 1; the pendulum, circle and spiral open Part IV and land in chapter 21; Klee ends in colour, so colour is taught as appearance at spine 4 and returns as energy with shaders (declared return, chapter 26).

Gaboury, Image Objects [V research_engine]: one technical object per chapter as a critique at chapter grain: culling (ch. 8), the default primitives / Utah teapot (ch. 3, 12), object orientation (ch. 15), frame buffer and GPU (ch. 16, 26).

Code as Creative Medium [V research_creative]: body-named assignments give the short track's mini project ('Extrapolated Body'); short exercises (PRIMM) against open assignments (Make); 'The Bimodal Classroom' for mixed groups at Konstfack.

SFPC Code Societies (3 weeks, a teacher per session) [V research_creative]: the short track's shape, with guest and critique sessions in week 3; it also shows how the late spine can be taught as critique beside code.
Queer Game Studies and CCS 382 [V research_queer]: failure before futures; the control's close runs crisis (37) to QFEP (38) to leaving the lab (39).

GDQuest Learn GDScript / 3D [V research_engine]: use before make (supplied walker, segment helper, XR staging, named and opened later); skin versus controller for swapping the desktop body for the XR body (chapter 12). The control does not take GDQuest's late _process: the spine teaches it at Point Zero.

Book of Shaders [V research_engine]: Ada's Shader halls follow its chapters 5-13 and the spine keeps its drawing-before-generative order; the control keeps shaders as one block at spine 12 and makes tiling-to-shader a declared return rather than a braided strand.

What no comparable course has, and the control keeps [V research_ccs, research_creative]: bodies built in 3D code, a falsifiable prediction per chapter, and the DEBT layer on geometry (polycount against deformation, the blob, stopped recursion). The canon's queer work is linguistic or data-centred; Ada's geometric queering is a gap the course should name, not borrow authority for.
